entries.title: Wishbone closing after 36 years, co-owners announce
entries.summary: <p>Wishbone Chicago is closing its doors after 36 years, the restaurant’s owners announced Monday morning.</p><p>“There is no easy way to say goodbye to something that has been such a large part of our lives for so long,” Joel and Julie Nickson said in an Instagram announcement. “To our many loyal customers and to the generations of staff members who helped make Wishbone what it became, thank you.”</p><p>The restaurant near the West Loop, at 161 N. Jefferson St., plans to remain open through the end of August, Joel Nickson told the Sun-Times. “It is sad, but I can’t complain. We had a good, long run.”</p><p>Monday was bustling at Wishbone with many customers coming in after hearing the news. Nickson was also busy trying to set up his 42 employees with new jobs. “A lot of them have been with me for a long time. It’s bittersweet,” he said. “A lot of the staff is like family. I’m sorry it has to end like this.”</p><p>A confluence of challenges led to Wishbone’s decision to close. It’s becoming “harder and harder” for independent restaurants to stay afloat, Nickson said.</p><p>Food and labor costs are up. On top of ongoing inflation, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/small-business/2025/02/05/chicago-restaurants-charging-extra-eggs-bird-flu-soaring-costs" target="_blank" ><u>egg costs</u></a> last year soared to the highest Nickson had seen in 35 years of running Wishbone. Egg costs eventually fell, but everything remains expensive, from repairs and deliveries to linens and utensils.</p><p>Wishbone has tried to pay its workers well. But various policies, such as Chicago’s hotly debated law to raise the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/work/2026/03/26/mayor-johnson-veto-freezing-tipped-minimum-wage-divides-restaurant-industry" target="_blank" ><u>tipped minimum wage</u></a> have increased pressure on owners. Labor costs are the “number one problem for restaurants now,” Nickson said. “You can only raise prices so much.”</p><p>Meanwhile, Wishbone’s business didn’t recover after the COVID-19 pandemic when offices shifted to remote work. “Friday used to be the busiest for lunch. But now it’s the slowest. Everybody takes Friday off,” Nickson said.</p><p>The economy remains tenuous and uncertain, so customers are spending less. “Money is tighter for everybody,” he said. Wishbone's catering business is also down.</p><p>In June, Wishbone had a major plumbing problem and it lost an entire weekend of business. </p><p>“My wife and I started realizing, we’re one disaster away from being in the hole. It’s better to pull the Band-Aid off now,” said Nickson. “It came to a point where it didn’t make sense for my wife and I to put in personal money to keep it going.”</p><p>The restaurant business has become more challenging, Nickson said.</p><p>“I’m glad I grew up when I did. Opening a restaurant now would be tough. For an independent, it would be a really hard road.”</p><p>Many loyal customers have been flocking to Wishbone since the announcement, including kids who used to sit in high chairs at the restaurant but are now adults. “People have been really upset. It brings tears to my eyes,” Nickson said.</p><p>Wishbone opened in 1990 at 1800 W. Grand Ave., moved to 1001 W. Washington Blvd. for 26 years and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2018/6/15/18445262/wishbone-has-found-a-new-west-loop-home" target="_blank" ><u>moved again</u></a> to 161 N. Jefferson St. near Fulton Market in 2018.</p><p>When Wishbone was on Washington in the heart of the West Loop, “we did very well over there in those days,” Nickson said. Basketball players and staffers from Oprah Winfrey’s Harpo Studios used to come to the restaurant. “It was a fun place.”</p><p>Wishbone is well known for its Southern-inspired cuisine. In a 1990 Sun-Times interview, then co-owner Maureen Murray said she and partner Joel Nickson used fresh seasonal ingredients.</p><p>“A lot of places say they are homestyle or Southern, but they don’t use anything fresh,” she said. “We do.”</p><p>Menu items from the time included grits for $1 and half a marinated chicken for $5.85.<br></p>

entries.title: Boy, 13, shot during attempted robbery in Washington Park
entries.summary: <p>A 13-year-old boy was shot during an attempted robbery Monday evening in Washington Park on the South Side, according to police.</p><p>The boy was near the back of a home around 7 p.m. in the 5800 block of South Michigan Avenue when he was approached by three people who tried to take his belongings, Chicago police said in a statement.. </p><p>One of the people pulled out a gun and hit the boy before firing, police said. The boy was shot in the ankle and taken to Comer Children's Hospital in good condition. </p><p>No arrests were made, police said.</p>

entries.title: Cubs want to rule baseball world, but after trade deadline, they still need to get past juggernaut Dodgers
entries.summary: <p>As <b>Jed Hoyer</b>, fresh off <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >win-now trade-deadline moves</a>, was lobbed a question about the Dodgers’ blockbuster trade for two-time Cy Young winner <b>Tarik Skubal</b>, he was accompanied by the Wrigley Field organ.</p><p>Though the organ plays only instrumentals, the lyrics of the '80s hit were unmissable:</p><p>“Everybody wants to rule the world.”</p><p>Only the Dodgers have ruled the baseball world for two years, and by adding Skubal, baseball’s most talent-rich team got richer, showing they have no intention of relinquishing the throne.</p><p>The Dodgers bested everyone for the summer’s top target, including the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>.</p><p>“We had a lot of conversations with them,” Hoyer said of unsuccessfully trying to pry Skubal from the Tigers.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/mlb/2026/08/03/brewers-trade-deadline-dustin-may-cubs-nl-central" >Brewers get starter Dustin May and 2 relievers in trade-deadline deals</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>With the Dodgers in town this week, the Cubs will get an up-close look at Skubal and an up-close look at what sits ahead of them as they chase their championship-level aspirations.</p><p>But for one night, at least, the Cubs showed how to depose the kings, smacking four homers, getting dazzling defense from <b>Pedro Ramirez</b> at third base and <b>Seiya Suzuki</b> in right field and watching starter <b>Matthew Boyd</b> throw 6 2/3 effective innings in a 10-5 win.</p><p>“It’s a tough team to beat, man,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said. “This is a really good baseball team, and you’ve got to play at your best to beat them. We showed a lot tonight.”</p><p>To win it all, though, they’ll have to beat the Dodgers in October.</p><p>Gulp.</p><p>“That’s the team you’ve got to beat, right?” Hoyer said. “Clearly, they’re going to be the favorites. They’ve won two times in a row. They’ve got the most talent in baseball, I don’t think there’s any question about that. It’s a great challenge for everybody.</p><p>“Going back to back is an incredible accomplishment, and I totally respect the fact that they pushed in to do it three times in a row. … It’s our job and everyone else’s job to make that not happen.”</p><p>The road to a World Series goes through Los Angeles, but the Cubs need to figure out how to get past their division rivals first. The Brewers are still seated comfortably at the top of the NL Central standings and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/25/cubs-playoffs-brewers-pirates-nl-central-matthew-boyd-starting-rotation" >knocked the Cubs out of the postseason last year</a>.</p><p>“The pressure’s on us,” Hoyer said. “We have to play really well to track them down.”</p><p>But the Dodgers are the team on everyone’s minds, their move to land Skubal casting them as an even more unstoppable juggernaut.</p><p>It infuriated a hefty percentage of baseball fans, if the boos from the Wrigley faithful were any indication.</p><p>“I know there’s been a reaction around baseball about it,” Hoyer said, “but they put themselves in position to do that deal. And they did. That’s exactly what they should be doing.”</p><h3><b>‘Moby Dick’ moment</b></h3><p>How long did Hoyer’s front office chase <b>Kevin Gausman</b>?</p><p>About as long as Captain Ahab chased Moby Dick.</p><p>The Cubs finally <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/02/dodgers-getting-tarik-skubal-only-makes-cubs-road-tougher" >landed the righty starter in a trade</a> Sunday.</p><p>“He was kind of a white-whale type target for us for a long time, going way back,” Hoyer said. “He kind of struggled early on [in his career], and we kept asking about him. … He went to San Francisco and took off.</p><p>“We were like, ‘Oh!’ We’d been asking about this guy for years thinking this is the talent he had. … He was a guy we really went after for a long time.”</p><h3><b>Shaw still stinging</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Utility man <b>Matt Shaw</b>’s long-lingering hand sprain is still smarting.</p><p>Shaw, sidelined since late June, hasn’t been able to take batting practice.</p><p>“The hope is certainly that he comes back this year and helps us,” Hoyer said.</p><h3><b>El Jaguar roars</b></h3><p>The Cubs swapped outfielders Monday, bringing <b>Kevin Alcantara</b> up from Triple-A Iowa and sending <b>Justin Dean</b> to the minors.</p><p>The move proved prescient: Alcantara slugged his first major league homer in the win.</p><p></p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-hide-descriptions="true" entries.title: Mayor Johnson's budget director Annette Guzman resigns
entries.summary: <p></p><p>Chicago Budget Director Annette Guzman abruptly resigned Monday, forcing Mayor Brandon Johnson to head into the all-important investors conference and a grueling election year budget season with a whole new financial team.</p><p>One week after Acting Chief Financial Officer Steven Mahr and Mahr’s top deputy <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/07/28/mayor-brandon-johnson-acting-cfo-steve-mahr-resigns" target="_blank" >jumped ship</a> without warning or explanation, Guzman followed them out the door.</p><p>What Secretary of State and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/08/02/alexi-giannoulias-chicago-mayor-candidate-2027-february-election-secretary-of-state" target="_blank" >mayoral contender Alexi Giannoulias</a> has called the “revolving door of senior leadership” under Johnson is spinning fast.</p><p>Ald. Matt O’Shea (19th) was part of the renegade coalition that rejected Johnson’s corporate head tax and passed an alternative, $16.7 billion budget with major elements that the mayor has never stopped fighting.</p><p>O’Shea said Guzman’s departure is the most surprising given the role she played in crafting and defending Johnson’s budget and battling the revenue items he didn’t like.</p><p>Her role as Johnson’s field general was on full display during a City Council hearing last month on the city’s mid-year financial report, O’Shea said.</p><p>During the hearing, Guzman and Mahr denied that foot-dragging on the very revenue items that Johnson opposes had caused a $90 million mid-year budget shortfall and warned of layoffs.</p><p>Citing late property tax payments from Cook County, they also hedged on whether the city could afford to make the second half of a $260 million advance pension payment that was at the center of the budget battle and, if so, how much that additional payment would be.</p><p></p><p>“When several of my colleagues and myself posed legitimate questions about our financial status, she was very defensive and very aggressive in her responses,” O’Shea said.</p><p>“She said there were no issues. The only issue was that the budget our coalition passed was to blame for this. She was very quick to point the finger. Now all of the sudden, she’s out the door.”</p><p></p><p>In addition to the $90-million mid-year shortfall, Chicago is facing a $1 billion budget gap next year and has a $36-billion pension crisis. Police and fire pension funds are hovering dangerously close to insolvency and needed a loan from the city to avoid selling assets to cover liabilities.</p><p></p><p>The question from investors assembling in Chicago for their annual meeting, and from Wall Street rating agencies that have already downgraded Chicago, is likely to be the same as the one that O'Shea is asking.</p><p>"Who's minding the store? What is going on? What is the mayor doing to get us on better financial footing?" O'Shea said</p><p>"The fact that he can't even retain his top financial team that he handpicked at this critical juncture should be alarming to everybody."</p><p></p><p>In a statement, Johnson thanked Guzman for her service. </p><p>"As Annette steps away from her role to focus on caring for her family, we are deeply grateful for all she has done for our City and wish her and her loved ones nothing but the very best. Family comes first, and we stand with her during this important time," Johnson said.</p><p>Finance Chair Pat Dowell (3rd) could not be reached for comment on Guzman's resignation.</p><p>Last week, Dowell all but blamed Guzman for Mahr's departure. She claimed that the acting CFO took “tons of shots for the administration when they basically hung him out to dry during hearings” before the City Council.</p><p></p><p>“When you step into a position like that, and you’re fairly junior, you need to have support, and I’m not sure he had that,” Dowell told the Sun-Times.</p><p>Asked whether it was Guzman who pulled the rug out from under Mahr, Dowell said, “Who is more senior? I couldn’t even point to somebody.”</p><p>O'Shea agreed with Dowell, telling the Sun-Times, “It’s become apparent to me that the budget director doesn’t play well with others in the sandbox. And we need a budget director, a comptroller and a chief financial officer working together.”</p>

entries.title: Brewers get starter Dustin May and 2 relievers in trade-deadline deals
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE — The Milwaukee Brewers had their sights set on acquiring a top-tier pitcher before the trade deadline — namely Tarik Skubal — but had to shift gears when the back-to-back AL Cy Young Award winner ended up with the Los Angeles Dodgers.</p><p>Instead, the Brewers, who entered Monday tied with the Dodgers for the best record in the major leagues, settled for veteran starter Dustin May, who was acquired from the St. Louis Cardinals shortly before the deadline.</p><p>Milwaukee also got left-handed reliever JoJo Romero in the deal. In exchange, the Brewers sent minor league outfielders Alexander Frías and Josiah Ragsdale to the Cardinals.</p><p>The NL Central leaders bolstered their bullpen further by obtaining reliever Antonio Senzatela from the Colorado Rockies for left-hander Mark Manfredi, who has split time between Double-A Biloxi and Triple-A Nashville, and infielder Juan Martínez, who has played with the Rookie ACL Brewers and Class A Wilson this season.</p><p>The Brewers entered Monday's games with a 6½-game lead over the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> in the division.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-jed-hoyer-top-prospects-trades-kevin-gausman-clay-holmes-ryan-zeferjahn-braxton-garrett-tyrone-taylor" >Jed Hoyer gets aggressive at trade deadline, deals prospects with Cubs’ present in mind: ‘We’re here to win’</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>"The fans have every right to have any opinion they want about what we should or shouldn't do," Milwaukee manager Pat Murphy said before Monday night's game against the Pittsburgh Pirates. "But nobody wants to win more than the guys in that (clubhouse)."</p><p>Murphy called prospects in the Brewers' highly touted minor league system the "lifeblood of an organization like ours."</p><p>"We're all working in a framework that has to make sense, so it's hard to make trades," he said.</p><p>General manager Matt Arnold said the Brewers "were in on a lot of things" as the deadline approached.</p><p>"There's certainly some things where you come up short, and you've just got to pick yourself up and dust yourself off and try to do what you can to get the next thing," Arnold said. "And ultimately, we were able to accomplish a lot over the last 48 hours that really helped the team."</p><p>Arnold declined to discuss the Brewers' failed effort to swing a deal for Skubal, who landed with the team that swept the Brewers in last season's National League Championship Series.</p><p>"I'm not going to talk about specific guys," Arnold said. "Obviously, we were in a lot of different things, and like I said, if you're able to access what you can, you get it, and if not, you move on."</p><p>The speculation on social media, the news media and elsewhere as the trade deadline approached has had a negative impact on his team, Murphy said.</p><p>"Everybody's aware of everything. Everybody hears names and all that kind of stuff," he said. "But we've got to go play baseball, and this has affected us. That's the reality. And I don't think it's healthy. We can't try to pretend it's not there. Can't lie to the players."</p><p>The Brewers' acquisitions will "help make us a bit stronger," Murphy said, noting that the team's pitching staff has been riddled with injuries.</p><p>Arnold expressed confidence that May, Romero and Senzatela, who were expected to arrive in Milwaukee late Monday or early Tuesday, will serve key roles as the Brewers look to reach the World Series for the first time since 1982.</p><p>"They're tough and they're experienced. They're going to fit in really well," Arnold said.</p><p>May, 28, went 5-7 with a 4.38 ERA in 21 starts for the Cardinals this season. He had 106 strikeouts in 109 innings. On May 27, May carried a no-hitter into the eighth at Milwaukee but ended up taking the loss as the Brewers rallied for a 2-1 win.</p><p>Over his eight-year major league career, he is 24-27 with a 3.99 ERA in 92 games (78 starts) with the Dodgers, Red Sox and Cardinals. May missed the 2024 season while recovering from his second Tommy John surgery and an esophageal tear. He has a mutual option for the 2027 season.</p><p>Brewers left-hander Kyle Harrison, a first-half standout who landed on the injured list July 11 with tightness in his pitching arm but is expected to return soon, overlapped with May in Boston and called him "a great guy with great stuff."</p><p>"It's just wicked sweepers, wicked sinker, changeups that fall off the table," Harrison said. "His stuff is nasty."</p><p>Romero, 29, was 1-3 with a 3.35 ERA in 44 relief appearances for the Cardinals this season. He is currently on the 15-day injured list recovering from an appendectomy. Romero has 43 strikeouts in 43 innings pitched and has stranded 20 of 28 inherited runners. He can become a free agent after the season.</p><p>Senzatela, 31, had spent his entire 10-year career with the Rockies, appearing in 212 games (145 starts). He has pitched exclusively in relief this season, going 9-2 with a 3.61 ERA and three saves in 34 appearances.<br></p>

entries.title: Boat sinks in Lake Michigan near 47th Street, injuring 3
entries.summary: <p>Three people were hospitalized after a boat capsized on Lake Michigan near Kenwood on Monday evening, according to the Chicago Fire Department.</p><p>The scuba team responded to a call of a boat sinking around 7 p.m. in the 4700 block of DuSable Lake Shore Drive, a department spokesperson said.</p><p>All seven people on the boat were pulled out of the water, the fire official said. Three and taken to a nearby hospital in good condition, while four others refused medical attention.</p><p>The boat was about 20 yards away from shore when it began to sink, the spokesperson said. No other information was immediately available.</p>

entries.title: White Sox GM Chris Getz accomplishes his goals; will that help players accomplish theirs?
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> general manager Chris Getz was beaming when he met with the media after the trade deadline passed Monday. Still, he was a bit tired.</p><p>‘‘Feel like I’ve gone through a day-night doubleheader myself,’’ he said.</p><p>Maybe three of them because Getz made his biggest move Saturday night, when he acquired right-hander Luis Castillo from the Mariners. He got an early start on deadline day, trading for Mets right-handed reliever Huascar Brazoban while most of Chicago was sleeping. In the daytime, he got two-time Gold Glove center fielder Brenton Doyle and Braves catcher Joey Bart.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/03/white-sox-acquire-braves-catcher-joey-bart-wholl-play-for-his-third-team-this-year" >White Sox acquire Braves catcher Joey Bart, who’ll play for his third team this year</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/08/03/white-sox-get-outfielder-brenton-doyle-from-rockies-for-two-prospects-including-pitcher-mason-adams" >White Sox get outfielder Brenton Doyle from Rockies for two prospects, including pitcher Mason Adams</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Getz achieved all of his goals before the deadline without giving up a prospect ranked among the top 100. He added a starting pitcher to help a rotation in need of length, a quality reliever, a right-handed bat for an outfield short on depth and a catcher. Yes, just a catcher.</p><p>But Getz achieving his goals doesn’t mean the Sox will achieve theirs. The moves have to work. Here’s what they mean:</p><p></p><h3>Bullpen</h3><p></p><p>Brazoban is in only his fifth major-league season, but he’s no spring chicken: He’s 36. Still, Getz raved about his performance in the World Baseball Classic, during which he struck out seven in four innings of relief for the Dominican Republic. He continued that success with the Mets, posting a 2.56 ERA in 52‰ innings with 49 strikeouts and 23 walks.</p><p></p><p>The Sox’ pen has been very good of late. Entering Monday, its 3.78 ERA and .229 opponents’ batting average ranked seventh in the majors, and the unit led all pens with 491 strikeouts. But it also ranked second with 502 innings, and Brazoban’s innings already rank third on the Sox. If he delivers, however, he might spell top relievers Sean Newcomb and Grant Taylor.</p><p></p><p>‘‘He takes the ball, has a great attitude,’’ Getz said. ‘‘Everyone I’ve talked to [says] he’s going to fit right in. Older guy, but he does have control. He’ll be able to pitch in leverage moments. Just an exciting get for us.’’</p><p></p><h3>Catcher</h3><p></p><p>Bart will play for his third team this season after starting with the Pirates and moving to the Braves. He was the No. 2 overall pick in the 2018 MLB Draft but hasn’t lived up to that billing. This season, he’s slashing .226/.303/.377 with four home runs in 41 games.</p><p></p><p>But that’s still more offense than the Sox have gotten from their catchers. Reese McGuire (no long with the team), Edgar Quero, Drew Romo and Kyle Teel have combined for a major-league-low .504 OPS. The next-closest team is the Yankees at .556.</p><p></p><p>Quero drew the short straw and was optioned to Triple-A Charlotte. So it’s Bart and Romo until Teel returns from a high ankle sprain, which the Sox are banking on.</p><p></p><p>‘‘We’re confident he’ll be back this season,’’ Getz said. ‘‘Kyle provides a lot, and we look forward to that time. In the meantime, we feel like we’ve got a catching group now that is only improved. And when Kyle comes back, it’s going to be another move.’’</p><p></p><h3>Center field</h3><p></p><p>Since returning from the break, All-Star Tristan Peters has a slash line of .098/.190/.118. Getz anticipates a platoon with the left-handed-hitting Peters and the right-handed-hitting Doyle, but he’ll leave that up to manager Will Venable. However they’re used, offense still might be an issue.</p><p></p><p>Doyle is slashing .214/.287/.282 with one homer in 45 games this season. He returned Friday from an oblique injury that cost him two months. His best season was in 2024, when he hit 23 homers, stole 30 bases and had an OPS+ of 102. Getz said he thinks the Sox can help Doyle, who’s under club control through 2029.</p><p></p><p>‘‘We see some offensive potential that hasn’t been tapped into recently,’’ Getz said. ‘‘Injuries are behind him. Our projections [say] if Brent Doyle comes to the White Sox, we’re going to add wins not only in 2026 but in 2027.’’</p><p></p><h3>Rotation</h3><p></p><p>Castillo will make his Sox debut Thursday in Boston, giving the team four quality starters with Anthony Kay, Davis Martin and Sean Burke. As for the fifth spot, the Sox</p><p>remain committed to rookie left-hander Noah Schultz. The question is for how long. The Sox are mindful that Schultz is close to his career high in innings, but Getz likes what he sees.</p><p></p><p>‘‘He can get really good lineups out,’’ Getz said. ‘‘You feel good when he’s starting. He’s still learning the major leagues. He does seem to be trending in a direction where he can be an impactful major-league starter. We’ve got some options if we need to give him a break.’’</p><p></p><p>Those include Triple-A starters David Sandlin, Shane Smith and Jose Urquidy and the Sox’ Erick Fedde, who moved to the bullpen upon Castillo’s arrival. For now, however, Schultz is No. 5.</p><p></p><p>‘‘We want to protect Noah Schultz just because of what he brings to this organization,’’ Getz said. ‘‘More than anything, when you bring in a [pitcher such as] Castillo, he gives us a little more breathing room and the ability to be creative with the group that we have.’’</p><p></p><h3>Sox at the trade deadline</h3><p><b>COMING</b></p><p>C Joey Bart entries.title: Jed Hoyer gets aggressive at trade deadline, deals prospects with Cubs’ present in mind: ‘We’re here to win’
entries.summary: <p>A year ago, the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2025/07/31/2025-trade-deadline-cubs-prez-jed-hoyer-balks-at-asking-price-for-frontline-starter-adds-four-players" >didn’t make a big splash at the trade deadline</a>.</p><p>Jed Hoyer’s front office saw the price of pitching and didn’t want to part with its top prospects, a decision that loomed large in hindsight, when pitching-depth issues helped the Cubs to an earlier-than-hoped playoff exit.</p><p>This year? Well, the same result won’t be for a lack of trying.</p><p>Hoyer & Co. went big this time around, parting with a half dozen of its top prospects — including No. 2 ranked infielder Jefferson Rojas, the No. 68 prospect in baseball — to bring in a trio of pitchers that can help the Cubs immediately. And, they hope, come October.</p><p>“Ideally, you don’t trade prospects,” Hoyer said after the deadline passed Monday. “But at the same time, we’re here to win.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-ryan-zeferjahn-bullpen-moises-ballesteros-trade-deadline-angels" >Cubs upgrade bullpen with Ryan Zeferjahn, give up Moises Ballesteros in trade with Angels</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-trade-deadline-clay-holmes-mets" >Cubs continue to bolster rotation, net Clay Holmes in swap with Mets</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Rojas was the cost of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-trade-deadline-clay-holmes-mets" >acquiring starting pitcher Clay Holmes</a> and reserve outfielder Tyrone Taylor from the Mets. The front office shipped away a quintet of top-30 prospects in <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/02/dodgers-getting-tarik-skubal-only-makes-cubs-road-tougher" >trades for starter Kevin Gausman</a>, reliever Ryan Zeferjahn and minor league starter Braxton Garrett, also parting with young slugger Moises Ballesteros <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/08/03/cubs-ryan-zeferjahn-bullpen-moises-ballesteros-trade-deadline-angels" >in the Zeferjahn deal</a>.</p><p>The two headlining acquisitions — rotation adds Gausman and Holmes — seem unlikely to be Cubs past the end of this season (Gausman’s contract is up, while Holmes has a player option), making Hoyer’s aggression all the more notable.</p><p>This goes back to the offseason, when the front office broke with the narrative by dealing outfield prospect Owen Caissie for starting pitcher Edward Cabrera and handing out a big-money, free-agent deal to third baseman Alex Bregman.</p><p>Combine those moves with the ones at the deadline, and the Cubs have acted on the belief that this team can win, win big and win right now.</p><p>“We’ve invested a lot in this roster, not just financially but in terms of how we put the roster together. It’s a really good team,” Hoyer said. “That’s part of being in contention and being in a good position. You have to make those decisions. You have to draft well, you have to develop well, and if you do those things, then you can afford to make those kinds of trades.”</p><p>Now it’s time to find out if the aggression will pay off.</p><p>Gausman, a two-time All Star, brings a milelong track record of big league success to the North Side, perhaps highlighted by the big innings he pitched for the Blue Jays as they fell just short of winning the World Series last October.</p><p>Holmes is a two-time All-Star reliever turned effective starter who had a 3.26 ERA in his season and a half with the Mets. He has been out since May recovering from a fractured fibula but is nearing a return, with three minor league rehab starts in the last week and a half.</p><p>Zeferjahn adds to what has been an injury-decimated Cubs bullpen, with a 1.38 ERA in his last 24 appearances since June 1. He was almost exclusively a late-inning arm for the Angels and figures to get those sorts of opportunities moving forward.</p><p>Taylor fits the bill of a righty bat off the bench, which Hoyer said was specifically requested by manager Craig Counsell with utility man Matt Shaw still nursing a lingering hand injury.</p><p>And Garrett, who made 30 effective starts for the Marlins in 2023, is a depth piece in the minor leagues (already sent to Triple-A Iowa) who could be helpful this year and into the future.</p><p>There are two months of regular-season baseball left — and, the Cubs hope, a month of postseason baseball after that — to find out if stepping on the gas in early August wins the race for this team.</p><p>The Brewers still hold a lead in the NL Central. And the in-town Dodgers are as tall a task to overcome as you’ll find, commanding as the back-to-back champs.</p><p>But Hoyer did his work at the deadline and reinforced a team that already owned one of the sport’s best records.</p><p>“In some ways, we were as focused as I can remember at a deadline,” he said. “It was very clear <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/17/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-starting-pitching-jed-hoyer-front-office" >we needed to add pitching</a>. … We wanted to add reinforcements, and we certainly did that.”</p><p></p><bsp-listcarousel class="PageListE" data-module data-column-count=3 data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" entries.title: After Mercury loss, Sky coach Tyler Marsh rips officiating of Kamilla Cardoso: 'It's a joke'
entries.summary: <p>It wasn't the reason the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> lost. Plenty of mistakes down the stretch cost them in Monday's 106-101 loss to the Mercury. And playing the fourth quarter without leading scorer Sydney Taylor, who exited with a left groin injury, didn't help.</p><p>But center Kamilla Cardoso once again played an entire game without attempting a free throw, and Sky coach Tyler Marsh couldn't believe it.</p><p>"It was a joke," Marsh said. "It's a [expletive] joke. How many more games does she need to go without getting a free throw? It makes no sense. Zero sense.</p><p>"Now, it didn't come down to that. We fouled our asses off today. We could have been more disciplined. Put them on the line 40 times. Not saying the officials made 40 wrong calls or 20 wrong calls or whatever it is. Not saying that at all.</p><p>"But for her to play as hard as she does consistently, she doesn't give much pushback to the officials. I try to talk as calmly as I can to officials before it gets out of hand. It's a joke."</p><p>Cardoso shot 8-for-15 for 16 points but never got to the line. Marsh has raised the issue throughout the season. After the Sky's win over the Sun last week, in which Cardoso got to the line 11 times, he made his point again.</p><p>"I can make a case that she should shoot close to 11 free throws every game," Marsh said. "I think she gets held a ton. I think that, for someone who shoots the majority of shots in the paint, there's just physically very little resistance that you can give without fouling her. She's just that forceful.</p><p>"To go games where she has zero to five free throws, it just doesn't make sense to me. And the film doesn't lie either."</p><p>Cardoso shoots 3.9 free-throw attempts per game, just 24th in the league, despite taking 9.7 shots per game in the paint, eighth most.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: All-Star Kelsey Plum lands in a new dimension, and the Sky had to pay for it
entries.summary: <p>A 12-point swing in the fourth quarter separated the Mercury and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> on Monday night at Wintrust Arena, with the former capitalizing on the mistakes of the latter to earn a 106-101 victory.</p><p>The trade deadline separated them even more: The Sky stood pat, while the Mercury swung for the fences.</p><p>The Mercury landed the biggest name on the market, acquiring five-time All-Star guard Kelsey Plum from the Sparks for young guard Monique Akoa Makani, a first-round draft pick in 2027 and a second-rounder in 2028. It was only the fourth time in league history an All-Star was traded in-season.</p><p>Mercury general manager Nick U’Ren framed the move as opportunistic.</p><p>‘‘I approach the [trade] deadline very opportunistically,’’ he said. ‘‘Sometimes that means selling, sometimes it means buying, sometimes it means a little bit of both. Every deadline is what deals come our way. This was something we wanted to pounce on.’’</p><p>Why the Mercury wanted Plum needs very little explaining. She’s one of the best scorers alive — she scored a cool 20 points off the bench in her first game in a Mercury uniform — and her work ethic is revered around the league.</p><p>The question was more about timing.</p><p>Plum will be a free agent after this season, and she reportedly wasn’t expected to stay in Los Angeles. The Mercury could have waited to court her in free agency and given up nothing. U’Ren signaled they wanted to cut the line and start pitching her now.</p><p>‘‘The chance to get Kelsey into our four walls and have her feel what we’re all about, have her feel our staff, our players and our organizational dynamic, was really important to us,’’ U’Ren said. ‘‘So we wanted to be aggressive in getting her here as early as possible.’’</p><p>U’Ren and coach Nate Tibbetts are hoping that Plum buys in for the long term and that it helps the Mercury’s playoff chances.</p><p>‘‘We’ve got to go on a run,’’ Tibbetts said. ‘‘We understand that. Our goal is to play good basketball. But we also want to make this a place that KP wants to be for a while. This isn’t just a 14- or 15-game rental in our mind; this is something we want to build upon.’’</p><p>Plum, meanwhile, is just getting her bearings. She was in shock when her agent called to tell her about the trade, and everything since has happened fast. She likened her last 48 hours to the Spider-Man multiverse.</p><p>‘‘It’s just a lot of different dimensions going,’’ she said.</p><p>Bringing her down to earth are some familiar faces. She played for Tibbetts with USA Basketball last fall and has won gold medals with Mercury stars Alyssa Thomas and Kahleah Copper on the national team.</p><p>Monday marked her return after a month out with a lower-leg injury. Even on a minutes restriction, she adapted seamlessly, going 3-for-5 from three-point range and dishing out four assists in addition to her 20 points.</p><p>‘‘When you play hard and compete, the game just opens up for you,’’ she said.</p><p>The Mercury entered the game in the same hole as the Sky. Both teams came into the season expected to make the playoffs. Both had injuries throw them off-course, with the Sky losing leading scorer Rickea Jackson and the Mercury playing most of the first half of the season without Sami Whitcomb.</p><p>Only one of them left Wintrust Arena with momentum. The victory moved the Mercury up to 10th place, still 5½ games out of a playoff spot. The Sky dropped to 11th and six games back with a loss they could ill-afford as they try to use this homestand to keep their playoff hopes alive.</p><p>‘‘It hurts, obviously, as a team that’s fighting for the same thing that we are,’’ Sky coach Tyler Marsh said. ‘‘They came onto our home court and took one, so it’s a credit to them. But for us, we’ve got two more opportunities to protect home court.’’</p><p>Sky point guard Courtney Vandersloot, who had a double-double but shouldered the blame for mistakes down the stretch, echoed the disappointment.</p><p>‘‘This obviously was a huge game just in where we are [and] where they are in the standings, everything,’’ Vandersloot said. ‘‘We knew how important this is. You score 101 points on your home floor, you're supposed to win. . . . This one hurts.’’</p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Couple's Relationship Teeters Above Oblivion
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I am in a relationship with my hot-and-cold fiance. I caught him cheating after we moved in together. He had been courting someone at work. I eventually forgave him. That was five years ago. In the time since, he has changed completely — for the worse.</p><p>He doesn't take me out, shows me no affection and rarely talks to me about anything except the bills. On top of that, we don't make love anymore. Is it because he got caught, or could he be cheating again? Either way, it doesn't matter. I've started to cheat, too. I don't care anymore. Should I kick him out and start over, or give it another chance? — <i>FRUSTRATED IN THE SOUTH</i></p><p><b>DEAR FRUSTRATED:</b> Let's review the things you have (and haven't) said in your letter. You allowed a man who cheated on you from the time he moved in to continue living with you. Since then, he doesn't take you out, shows you no affection and is no longer inclined to make love with you. The reason isn't because you caught him cheating. It's because he isn't in love with you!</p><p>Whether he's seeing other women is no longer relevant because you aren't faithful to him either. Why you would give this relationship another chance is beyond me. Not once in your letter did you say you love him. It's time to end it. Then do what you can to heal from this sorry experience (including consulting a licensed counselor if one is available) and move on with your life.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband and I just had our first child. He is less than 3 months old. We live close to our family and get together often. My sister and her husband have two sons, 3 and 1. They are constantly sick. My sister and her husband have a history of downplaying their illnesses so that they don't miss out on family events. They always show up, and even before we had a child, it made us uncomfortable. Now that we have a vulnerable baby, it's become not only reckless but dangerous.</p><p>When their kids arrive sick, they cough all over everything, and they are never encouraged to wash their hands or cover their mouths when they do it. How do we express our concern to my sister and her husband without sounding like overbearing parents? — <i>CONCERNED NEW MOTHER</i></p><p><b>DEAR MOTHER:</b> Congratulations on your new baby! Infants under 6 months old are prone to severe complications from colds and other viruses, so you need to do more than "express your concern." Stop letting sick people near your new son.</p><p>If the gathering is at someone's home, designate a "baby room" where people with coughs and sneezes are not allowed, and everyone must wash up before entering. Take turns with your husband sitting with the baby in the safe space, or even hire a (healthy) sitter to stay in the room with your son. If people tease you or call you overbearing, so be it. Your baby, your rules.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p>
entries.author: Abigail Van Buren

entries.title: Illinois lawmakers decry prison's 'gut-wrenching,' 'heartbreaking' conditions
entries.summary: <p>Illinois lawmakers are calling for changes at the Joliet Treatment Center, after a Marshall Project, Chicago Sun-Times and WBEZ investigation exposed an epidemic of fires that resulted in two deaths at the prison.</p><p>In the last three years, there have been more than 70 fires at the prison, including a dozen cases of self-immolation, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2026/07/24/joliet-prison-fires-mental-health-illinois-department-corrections" >the investigation</a> found.</p><p>Despite the prevalence of fires, the facility in Joliet failed to have working fire alarms, to provide evacuation plans to fire officials or to allow ambulances to quickly enter and leave prison grounds, according to government records.</p><p>“The highest levels of administration are so incompetent, and it's just a shame,” said<u> </u>state Sen.Terri Bryant, a Republican based in Murphysboro. “People's lives are in jeopardy.”</p><p>Bryant, who worked in corrections for 20 years, said it’s not just incarcerated people who are at risk. People employed at the facilities are also exposed to smoke and don’t have the proper equipment to respond to blazes.</p><p>State Sen. Robert Peters, D-Chicago, called on administrators at the Illinois Department of Corrections to act.</p><p>“It is more critical now than ever for the center’s administrators to implement adequate fire safety infrastructure, create an effective fire evacuation plan and ensure emergency responses are handled with the timeliness they deserve,” said Peters. “People’s lives are on the line.”</p><p>The state opened the Joliet Treatment Center in 2017 to provide treatment to people in prison who have serious mental illnesses. It initially won praise for offering robust therapy and support. But conditions began declining, and men held there reported that they struggled to get physical and mental healthcare, and were left to spend long stretches locked in their cells. Desperate for help, they began setting their cells — or bodies — on fire.</p><p>Gov. JB Pritzker declined to comment on the investigation, instead pointing to a statement issued by the Department of Corrections.</p><p>The department had also refused to answer questions about fire preparedness at the Joliet Treatment Center, but a spokesperson wrote in a statement that the agency is “committed to ensuring the safety and security of staff, individuals in custody and all persons who enter our facilities.”</p><p>Illinois state Sen. Rachel Ventura, a Democrat who represents Joliet, where the prison is located, called the investigation's findings heartbreaking and demanded an audit of the department’s procedures and better training for its staff.</p><p>State Rep. Lindsey LaPointe, D-Chicago, said the problems at the Joliet Treatment Center are especially gut-wrenching given the facility's mission to provide services to people with mental health needs.</p><p>“Policymakers and residents want mental health care access for all Illinoisans, and this must include people with severe mental health conditions who are overrepresented in jails and prisons due to our policy failures,” said LaPointe.</p><p>Destinee Ortiz, a county board member in Will County where the prison is located, wrote Pritzker <a class="Link" href="https://www.instagram.com/p/DbYmhoSDqHp/" target="_blank" ><u>a public letter</u></a> and asked what will be done to address the fatal fires. “A facility built to provide treatment and hope should not be the subject of findings like these,” she wrote.</p><p>In one case highlighted in the investigation, a man named Jason Stephens set a fire in his cell and then was left locked in it for a half-hour.</p><p>When firefighters reached Stephens and tried to take him to the hospital, the prison’s guards refused to open the gate for the ambulance for nearly 28 minutes. In prison reports, they said they were waiting on paperwork and a guard to accompany Stephens to the hospital.According to one guard, a firefighter said to prison employees, “This man can die while y’all pussyfooting around.”</p><p>Two weeks later, Stephens died of his injuries from the fire.</p><p>State Rep. Kevin Olickal, D-Chicago, said tragedies like Stephens’ death “highlight the urgent need for independent oversight” of the state’s prisons and said legislators have a duty to act.</p><p>The John Howard Association, a prison watchdog group, has been calling for such oversight of the department for years.</p><p>“These are public institutions, closed though they may be,” said the organization's executive director, Jenny Vollen-Katz, in a response to the investigation. “They should have all of the same safeguards that other public spaces have.”</p><p>Terah Tollner, a lawyer and representative for Stephens’ family, said she was horrified to learn of the many warning signs that the Department of Corrections had ignored, and called on the governor to take action.</p><p>“As the reporting makes clear, Jason Stephens did not have to die,” she said.</p>

anti-violence volunteer is set to go on trial Monday on gun charges that could send him to prison for decades.</p><p>Smith, a convicted felon, was arrested March 4, 2023, after officers found a loaded exchange for a $100 Visa gift card.</p><p>But the gift cards are available only during scheduled gun turn-in events. The Calumet District station wasn't hosting one when Smith arrived.</p><p>The city’s guidelines state that a person can surrender a gun at a police station at any time, or call 911 or 311, even when no turn-in event is underway.</p><p>Smith insists the police report gets the story wrong.</p><p>He said he owns a business that cleans out homes and he also operates three community gardens on the South Side.</p><p>In March 2023, he said, a woman from Atlanta hired his company to remove belongings from her late father’s home.</p><p>One of Smith’s workers took a handgun from a pile of possessions and hid it in Smith’s truck, he said.</p><p>Smith said he discovered the gun after stopping for lunch at Popeyes.</p><p>He tried to reach the woman who’d hired him but got no response. He then called 311 and was told he could take the gun to a church or police station, he said.</p><p>“I said, ‘Well, it’d be better for me to take it to the police because that’s showing integrity, you know what I’m saying?’" Smith recalled.</p><p>He said he put the gun in his coat pocket because he didn't want to walk into a police station carrying it in his hand.</p><p>His plan, he said, was to ask for a supervisor and hand over the entire jacket.</p><p>But when he told a desk officer he wanted to surrender a gun, she yelled, “Freeze!”</p><p>“The whole police station panicked and I got 10 guns aimed at me,” Smith said.</p><p>He denied ever asking about the $100 gift cards.</p><p>Despite acknowledging that he possessed the gun, Smith believes a jury will understand why.</p><p>“All we can do is convince them that, ‘Hey, he made the right decision, even though he broke the law,’” he said.</p><p>Smith said he rejected a plea deal that would have required him to serve two years in prison.</p><p>“God is on my side,” he said. “God guided me inside that police station. God protected me when I had all these guns faced at me and God is gonna protect me at the end of the day because I saved a life” by surrendering the weapon.</p><p>The Cook County state's attorney's office said "combating gun violence is a top priority.</p><p>"We make charging decisions based on our review of the evidence and the facts. The CCSAO is committed to prosecuting all cases while ensuring fairness, integrity and due process for everyone involved. We do not comment on the specifics of pending cases. In all cases, we consider mitigating factors to seek an appropriate outcome."</p><p>Duncan said he learned of the case only a few weeks ago.</p><p>He said Smith has stayed out of trouble for years since completing a prison sentence for a felony drug conviction.</p><p>“He’s not just a citizen,” Duncan said. “He’s fighting for good. He’s helping to push the peace.”</p><p>Duncan warned that convicting Smith could discourage others from surrendering unwanted guns.</p><p>“We’re most concerned about the travesty or injustice to him,” he said. “But the larger message is, since the community already doesn’t trust the police, they’re already skeptical. They’re going to be like, ‘No, we’re not going to do that, I know what happened to Nakia, no way I’m going to put myself in that position.’ Why would anybody risk their own freedom to turn in a entries.title: Intruder scrawls racist message inside Brighton Park home; cops investigate as possible hate crime
entries.summary: <p>Police are investigating a hate crime after a Brighton Park home was vandalized Monday.</p><p>Officers were called around 9 a.m. after the owner arrived at the house he is renovating in the Southwest Side neighborhood. Inside, he had found racist graffiti, according to a police report obtained by the Sun-Times. Someone had written “F*ck China” in black paint on a wall, the report said. The owner is a man of Asian descent.</p><p>There was other damage inside as well. The owner told police the intruders had damaged three electrical panels and removed copper pipes. He told officers he believed the intruder may have used a ladder to enter the home through a second-floor window and left through the home's front door.</p><p>No arrests have been made.<br></p>

entries.title: Bodies of 2 Chicago-area kayakers found off island in Door County
entries.summary: <p>The bodies of two 20-year-old Chicago-area kayakers were recovered in the waters off Washington Island, a popular tourist destination in Door County, Wisconsin, officials announced Monday. </p><p>The kayakers — David Thalman of Dundee and Francesca Warick of South Elgin — went missing near the island, and on Sunday rescue efforts turned into a recovery mission, according to the Door County sheriff's office. </p><p>Recovery operations continued throughout Monday with personnel from the Washington Island Police Department, Gibraltar Police Department, Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources and the Door County Sheriff's Office leading efforts in kayakers' last known location.</p><p>Thalman's body was found around 10:55 a.m. Monday, according to the sheriff's office. A short time later, searchers found Warick's body. Drowning may have been the primary cause of death, officials said. </p><p>Washington Island, home to about 600 people, is reached by a 5-mile ferry ride from the northeast tip of the Door Peninsula in Door County across the once-treacherous waters of Death’s Door, where Green Bay and Lake Michigan meet, according to Destination Door County's website. Visitors can tour remote parks, lavender and cherry farms and attend island festivals. </p><p>The Door County Sheriff’s Office said it is continuing to investigate.</p>

entries.title: Man seriously wounded in Near West Side shooting that forced lane closures on Dan Ryan
entries.summary: <p>A man was seriously wounded early Tuesday in a shooting that forced lane closures on the Dan Ryan Expressway on the Near West Side. </p><p>The man was shot multiple times around 3 a.m. in the 1200 block of South Ruble Street, Chicago police said. </p><p>He was taken to Stroger Hospital where he was in serious condition, police said. A description of the attacker was not given. </p><p>Inbound lanes on the Dan Ryan Expressway near the shooting scene were closed temporarily and reopened around 4:40 a.m., according to Illinois State Police. </p><p>CPD Area 3 detectives were investigating. </p>

anti-violence volunteer?</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wukkkuk-l-k/" target="_blank" >Frank Main</a></h5><p><b>Future at risk</b>: Nakia Smith says he walked into the Calumet District police station to get a gun off the street. Instead, he walked out in handcuffs. Three years later, the 51-year-old anti-violence volunteer is set to go on trial next week on gun charges that could send him to prison for decades.</p><p><b>The details</b>: Smith, a convicted felon, was arrested March 4, 2023, after officers found a loaded .45-caliber handgun in his coat pocket inside the police station. He says he was there to surrender the weapon. Police say he was breaking the law because felons can't possess guns. Smith said he believed the Chicago Police Department's gun turn-in program allowed people to surrender weapons anonymously and without fear of arrest.</p><p><b>Getting involved</b>: The case has stunned former U.S. Education Secretary Arne Duncan, who now runs the Chicago CRED anti-violence group, where Smith volunteers. "It’s crazy," Duncan said. "If I didn’t know his character, I wouldn’t be involved. But it seems like a complete, complete travesty."</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wukkkuk-l-u/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>SPRINGFIELD ✶</h4><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-830000" name="image-830000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4fe2d91/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7535x4229+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F54%2F9e%2F1420870843b7be94084ba0047f34%2Fpritzkerbudget-260627-23.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a37a866/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7535x4229+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F54%2F9e%2F1420870843b7be94084ba0047f34%2Fpritzkerbudget-260627-23.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/94e4018/2147483647/strip/true/crop/7535x4229+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F54%2F9e%2F1420870843b7be94084ba0047f34%2Fpritzkerbudget-260627-23.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Illinois House Speaker Emanuel "Chris" Welch speaks at a June 16 news conference. podcast</a></h3><p></p><h5>Reporting by <a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wukkkuk-l-ij/" target="_blank" >Mariah Woelfel</a></h5><p>Musician and comedian Al Scorch thinks he got the "last gasp" of an old-school childhood growing up in the 1980s and '90s on Chicago’s blue-collar Northwest Side.</p><p>That "last gasp" was more like a deep inhale that shaped Scorch into a Chicagoan's Chicagoan with an imaginative sense of humor and authoritative knowledge of the city. He's been exhaling Chicago-centric creative projects that have gained him tens of thousands of followers in the decades since.</p><p>Now, Scorch is embarking on a major endeavor: to read the entire municipal code of Chicago aloud for a podcast in an iconic Chicago accent.</p><p>The accent is an exaggeration of his own vernacular, honed in alleys and parks growing up with friends who would imitate the adults in their lives as comedic relief.</p><p>"It was this way of making fun of these adults who would be kind of jerks to us," Scorch said. "You know they’d be like, 'Don’t-ch-you kids go messin' 'round wit' my garbage cans!' And you’re just like — that's the funniest thing I’ve ever heard."</p><p>Scorch plans to release weekly episodes reciting the code, which governs everything from how tall you can grow your parkway plants to how the city defines bodily autonomy.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://newsletters.suntimes.com/t/t-l-wukkkuk-l-it/" target="_blank" ><b>READ MORE</b></a></p><hr><p></p><h4>YOUR DAILY QUESTION ☕️</h4><p>How would you describe the "Chicago accent" — and where in the city can you hear it?</p><p><a class="Link" href="mailto:newsletters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" ><i>Reply to this question via email</i></a><i> (please include your first and last name). target="_blank" >Privacy Policy</a></p> </div> </form> </bsp-form> </div> </div><p>The action starts when Ben (John Gawlik) hears from his friend Art (Paul D’Addario) that he has had an erotic dream about Ben’s wife. In the dream, Ben’s wife, Catherine (Brittany Burch), has golden spun hair and commits the deed in a room made of marble. When Ben tells Catherine about the dream, she reveals she had the same dream.</p><p>The overarching theme of the production: Marriage kind of sucks. We meet two upper middle class urban couples who are all clearly unhappy with the monotonous nature of their lives. But they have a cavalier acceptance of their mundane existence that brings an offbeat feel to the show while also making the stakes (marriage, infidelity, death) feel unusually low.</p><p>Even when characters contemplate suicide, or envision their own soon-coming natural deaths, it comes across as plainly as doing dishes or any other unenjoyable yet necessary household chore.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-330000" name="module-330000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3><a class="Link" href="https://thegifttheatre.org/event/marble-a-chicago-premiere-by-marina-carr/2026-07-30/" target="_blank" ><b><u>“Marble”</u></b></a></h3><b>When:</b> Through Aug. 30<br><b>Where:</b> The King’s Hall in the Copernicus Center, 5216 W. Lawrence<br><b>Info:</b> Tickets from $50</div> </div><div class="RatingCard Enhancement" data-module data-rating="3.5" data-align-center> <div class="RatingCard-content"> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star"> <span class="RatingCard-star-full"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> <span class="RatingCard-star-half"> <svg class=""> <use xlink:href="#icon-star"></use> </svg> </span> </span> </div> </div><p>But this show still works, for two reasons. One is the acting, by a cast entirely composed of Gift ensemble members that breathe life into charters that would otherwise feel flat. The other is the direction of Kay Martinovich, who clearly understood what Carr wanted to get across with this script. Even though it was written about 20 years ago, the story feels fresh in Martinovich’s hands.</p><p>Ultimately, the play is about women — specifically, middle class housewives. It explores the roles women are expected to play domestically, and how their married lives become reduced to a perpetual cycle of caretaking and housekeeping. Inevitably, their individualism is so swallowed up that they disappear into a shell of sadness that no else seems to see.</p><p>Martinovich crystalizes these ideas with her staging. Characters who are not in scenes often remain on stage. They are ghosts wallowing in the shadows of the impending doom that will eventually come to the realization that they have all stopped living life many years ago. The fact that this production earns so many audible laughs is both a testament to Carr and stark social commentary on the roles of women and the ease in which audiences will recognize their plight.</p><p>At one point, Ben tells Catherine, “women who can’t ovulate should die offstage,” which earns a room resounding gasp followed by chuckles.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>“Marble” asks existential questions about dreams and reality.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Joe Mazza</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Burch is excellent as Catherine. Her monologues are poetic in language but sharp in wit and emotion. Her downward spiral is haunting. The repeated dreams of Art eventually push her over the edge, but over time, it’s revealed that she had always been teetering.</p><p>Cyd Blakewell is equally as impressive as Art’s wife, Anne, a housewife who lives on three glasses of wine per day. Once the dreams start, she recognizes something is off with Art but simply asks him to keep her oblivious. As an actor, Blackwell has a keen gift that emerges throughout her performances. She can convey more feelings with her facial expressions than most of us can with words.</p><p>The play asks existential questions about dreams and reality. The characters, particularly Catherine and Anne, are so flippant with their own morality – to them, death is always around the corner, and with a life so unfulfilling, why care? The rub here is that if they don’t care, how can the audience?</p><p>At times, this sort of fatalism makes it hard to invest in the stakes of the characters, whose marriages are ripped apart by these fantasies. The comedic nature of the script, paired with a casual approach to impending doom, makes it a little difficult to react to the inevitable final scenes, yet again, the fine acting makes it work.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a60000" name="image-a60000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Paul D’addario and Cyd Blakewell play married couple Art and Anne.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Courtesy of Joe Mazza</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>What the production does well is spur reflection. Catherine dreaming about Art, and not being able to have him, is all too relatable. For me, I watched her dreams about Art, and her discussions about the road-not-taken, and all the could-have-beens, and thought about my own “art.” In my case, it's the unfinished screenplay on my laptop. Here, the characters' dreams infiltrate their realities, and in the end, make some of them wonder whether their actual lives were even worth living.</p><p>In the end, the play itself is like a marriage that goes off the rails. The crash is tragic, but as a spectator, you can’t take your eyes off it.</p>

entries.title: Man killed, woman wounded in South Chicago shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man who was killed last month has been identified after the shooting that also left a woman wounded in the South Chicago neighborhood.</p><p>Jose Ariel Gonzalez, 40, and a 32-year-old woman were in the 8900 block of South Escanaba Avenue around 3:05 a.m. July 26 when they were both shot, Chicago police and the Cook County medical examiner's office said. </p><p>Gonzalez was shot in his neck and taken to the University of Chicago Medical Center where he died, police said. The woman was shot in her chest and went to Trinity Hospital where she was in good condition. </p><p>Area 4 detectives were investigating. </p>

entries.title: Giannoulias se postula para alcalde de Chicago y afirma que Johnson ‘no ha estado a la altura del momento’
entries.summary: <p>Apuntando al vaivén del liderazgo en la alcaldía de Brandon Johnson, el secretario de Estado de Illinois, Alexi Giannoulias, se sumó el domingo a la carrera por la alcaldía, presentándose como alguien que construye coaliciones para resolver los enormes problemas de Chicago.</p><p>Giannoulias entra a la contienda como presunto favorito con un objetivo político marcado en la espalda, después de haber recaudado $22 millones de líderes empresariales y de ganarse el apoyo de los sindicatos del sector obrero.</p><p>Con el riesgo de morder la mano que alimentó su campaña, Giannoulias se comprometió a respaldar el impuesto a los millonarios que Johnson también ha defendido.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-350000" name="module-350000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>Pero, a diferencia de Johnson, que ha usado presupuestos anteriores para reducir al Departamento de Policía de Chicago, Giannoulias prometió contratar a 1,000 oficiales de policía adicionales para 2030 y reinstaurar ShotSpotter, el contrato de tecnología para detección de disparos que Johnson canceló. Johnson ha criticado la efectividad de ShotSpotter y ha dicho que quiere destinar el gasto a medidas preventivas.</p><p>Giannoulias sostuvo que el liderazgo de Johnson “no ha estado a la altura”, aunque “su corazón está en el lugar correcto”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-073db0" name="image-073db0"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/b40cce8/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5d%2F11%2F53719dc0440cb0769c8452daeb17%2Fcouncil-260521-15.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/4f80835/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5d%2F11%2F53719dc0440cb0769c8452daeb17%2Fcouncil-260521-15.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ed40a92/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5d%2F11%2F53719dc0440cb0769c8452daeb17%2Fcouncil-260521-15.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="El alcalde Brandon Johnson revisa pantallas durante una reciente votación del Concejo Municipal en el ayuntamiento en el Loop. Aún no ha dicho si se postulará de nuevo para alcalde." srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ed40a92/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5d%2F11%2F53719dc0440cb0769c8452daeb17%2Fcouncil-260521-15.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/0567f63/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5d%2F11%2F53719dc0440cb0769c8452daeb17%2Fcouncil-260521-15.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/ed40a92/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+0/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5d%2F11%2F53719dc0440cb0769c8452daeb17%2Fcouncil-260521-15.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>El alcalde Brandon Johnson revisa pantallas durante una reciente votación del Concejo Municipal en el ayuntamiento en el Loop. Aún no ha dicho si se postulará de nuevo para alcalde.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Jeremy Battle/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>En un acto de lanzamiento de campaña el domingo, sonó un popurrí de música con temática de Chicago, entre ellas “Sweet Home Chicago” y “End of Beginning” de Djo, mientras los simpatizantes llegaban a la sede del sindicato IBEW Local 134 en el vecindario de Bronzeville.</p><p>Entre la marea de personas con camisetas naranjas que decían “LiUNA Local 1001 for Alexi” estaban los concejales Félix Cardona Jr. (31.°), Emma Mitts (37.°), Timmy Knudsen (43.°), Michelle Harris (8.°) y Brian Hopkins (2.°).</p><p>Aunque Giannoulias no entró en detalles sobre las ideas clave que expuso en un video de anuncio el domingo —pre-kinder universal, reforma del impuesto a la propiedad y aumento del salario mínimo—, dijo a la multitud que cree “fundamentalmente que el gobierno puede ser competente y compasivo, y eso es lo que llevaré al Ayuntamiento”.</p><p>“Les pido que vuelvan a creer —que crean que el gobierno puede, una vez más, ser digno de las personas a las que sirve”, dijo. “Juntos escribiremos el próximo capítulo de la mejor ciudad del mundo, así que hagámoslo juntos”.</p><p>Giannoulias dijo al Chicago Sun-Times en una entrevista amplia que la “administración se ha convertido en una puerta giratoria de altos mandos, lo que hace más difícil que la Ciudad haga las cosas, reduce la confianza en la Ciudad —y todo el mundo lo ve”.</p><p>El liderazgo efectivo requiere “formar coaliciones y trabajar con la gente”, y Johnson “está fallando en eso”, dijo Giannoulias.</p><p>“Enfrentamientos con el gobernador. Exigir cosas al final en lugar de trabajar antes para desarrollar políticas y construir apoyos… Su intento de subir los impuestos a la propiedad fue rechazado por el Concejo Municipal 50 a 0 y el Concejo aprobó un presupuesto 29 a 19 cuando él no retrocedió del impuesto corporativo per cápita”, dijo Giannoulias.</p><p>“Un alcalde que no puede impulsar una agenda en Springfield y en el Concejo Municipal tiene dificultades… para velar por los intereses de los habitantes de Chicago”.</p><p>La renuncia abrupta del director financiero de la Ciudad, Steve Mahr, y de su principal adjunto —justo cuando Chicago se prepara para recibir una crucial conferencia de inversionistas y el Concejo se alista para una agotadora temporada presupuestaria electoral— es el ejemplo más reciente de la “puerta giratoria” de Johnson en el Ayuntamiento, dijo Giannoulias.</p><p>“Contrató a un veterano de larga trayectoria en la ciudad como Rich Guidice para que tuviera una mano firme cuando fue elegido, y se fue en menos de un año de la administración. El superintendente de policía [Larry] Snelling renunció con menos de un año restante en esta administración, que es la época más desafiante del año para la policía”, dijo Giannoulias.</p><p>“Tres agencias hermanas estuvieron sin líder por más de un año: las Escuelas Públicas de Chicago (CPS), la Autoridad de Vivienda de Chicago (CHA) y la Autoridad de Tránsito de Chicago (CTA). Y después de pasar casi diez años sin una degradación de calificación crediticia, Chicago ha… sido degradada por tres agencias calificadoras en poco más de un periodo de tres años”.</p><div Educación de Chicago</a> de jugársela y aprobar un presupuesto de casi $10,000 millones que cuenta con $150 millones procedentes de Springfield. La junta lo hizo en contra de los deseos de la superintendente de CPS, Macquline King, aunque su propuesta —y la versión que aprobó la junta— también contaba con un superávit de $285 millones por financiamiento por incremento de impuestos (TIF) que el Concejo Municipal no ha aprobado.</p><p>Giannoulias lo llamó otra señal de que el Sindicato de Maestros de Chicago (CTU), que financió y proveyó personal para la campaña de Johnson en 2023, está marcando la pauta en su administración.</p><p>“En lugar de adoptar el presupuesto propuesto por la directora ejecutiva de las [Escuelas Públicas de Chicago], que incluía recortes de personal, los miembros vinculados al CTU impusieron a la fuerza este presupuesto alternativo, que evita cualquier elección difícil sobre cambios estructurales. Eso no es liderazgo”, dijo Giannoulias. “Trabajaré con la presidenta de la junta para abogar por más fondos. Pero tenemos que empezar por un presupuesto más responsable… Posibles ingresos brillantes no son responsables”.</p><h3>La posibilidad de cierres de escuelas</h3><p>Giannoulias dijo que un presupuesto escolar más responsable debe confrontar al elefante financiero en la sala: 145 escuelas con más asientos vacíos que estudiantes.</p><p>Si es elegido alcalde, se compromete a abordar ese problema, pero con un proceso impulsado por la comunidad y los padres “acompañado de una inversión real en estudiantes y personal... no cierres impuestos desde el centro con poca antelación”.</p><p>“Los cierres pasados, en particular en 2013, se manejaron de una manera que rompió la confianza con las comunidades negras y latinas, y esa historia no puede ser ignorada ni repetida”, dijo Giannoulias.</p><p>Johnson señala la decisión del exalcalde Rahm Emanuel de cerrar 50 escuelas de golpe en 2013 como un ejemplo de desinversión flagrante en las comunidades del los lados sur y oeste.</p><p>Pero, aún arriesgándose a ser presentado como Emanuel 2.0, Giannoulias dijo que “hay que tomar decisiones difíciles… Una escuela con muy pocos estudiantes no puede ofrecer la gama completa de programas… La experiencia del estudiante no es la misma. No es un ambiente sano para que 70 u 80 estudiantes estén en una escuela diseñada para 1,500. No es bueno para nadie”.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f20db6"
