waste.</p><p>“If I can find something to donate to my kid's school that would be great, or donate to any of the teacher giveaways that are happening in preparation for the new school year,” Parchem said.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://www.facebook.com/share/p/1CBaDyQpcG/" target="_blank" ><u>online posts about the</u></a> dumpsters drew the ire of parents who accused Chicago Public entries.title: One of tabbouleh-inspired salad’s greatest strengths is its make-ahead convenience
entries.summary: <p>Bring this vibrant salad to your next picnic, potluck or backyard barbecue. Inspired by the bright, herb-forward flavors of traditional Middle Eastern tabbouleh, this hearty variation replaces bulgur with fluffy couscous and adds roasted eggplant and crumbled feta for extra substance and depth. The result is a colorful, satisfying dish that can stand alone as a vegetarian meal or shine alongside grilled foods.</p><p>Tender, lightly charred eggplant lends a silky texture and subtle smokiness that complements the couscous, while lemon juice, olive oil and a generous handful of fresh herbs infuse every bite with brightness. Crumbled feta adds a salty tang, and a touch of chile brings pops of heat that balance the salad's citrusy notes.</p><p>One of this salad's greatest strengths is its make-ahead convenience. In fact, it benefits from a little resting time, allowing the flavors to meld and the herbs to perfume the couscous. Serve it at room temperature for the best flavor and texture. While preparation involves a bit of chopping, the effort is well rewarded. Be especially generous with the parsley, mint and other fresh herbs; the couscous readily absorbs their flavors, ensuring that every forkful is fragrant, lively and refreshing.</p><p>Colorful and packed with contrasting textures, this couscous salad is a crowd-pleasing dish that brings the spirit of tabbouleh to any warm-weather gathering.</p><h3>Charred Eggplant Couscous Salad</h3><p><b>Active time:</b> 45 minutes<br><b>Total time:</b> 45 minutes, plus cooling time<br><b>Yield:</b> Serves 6</p><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p><b>Eggplant</b><br>3 to 4 small or Italian eggplants, about 1 pound<br>Olive oil<br>Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper</p><p><b>Couscous</b><br>1 1/2 cups water<br>1 1/2 cups couscous<br>2 tablespoons olive oil, plus more as needed<br>1 teaspoon kosher salt, or more as needed<br>1 large garlic clove, grated<br>2 tablespoons fresh lemon juice<br>1 teaspoon finely grated lemon zest, plus more for garnish<br>1 teaspoon ground cumin<br>1 teaspoon ground coriander<br>1/2 teaspoon sweet paprika<br>1/4 teaspoon cayenne<br>1 medium red bell pepper, seeded and finely diced<br>1 small red chile, such as Fresno, seeded and finely diced<br>1 cup chopped flat-leaf parsley leaves<br>1 cup chopped cilantro leaves<br>1/2 cup mint leaves, plus additional leaves for garnish<br>1/3 cup crumbled feta cheese</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Trim the ends of the eggplants, then slice lengthwise, about 1/4 inch thick. Generously brush the slices with olive oil and season with salt and black pepper.</p><p>If grilling, cook the eggplants over direct medium heat until soft and charred on both sides, turning once or twice, 6 to 8 minutes. Alternatively, heat the oven to 425 degrees. Arrange the eggplant slices in one layer on a rimmed baking sheet lined with parchment. Roast until soft and charred in spots, 12 to 15 minutes, flipping once.</p><p>Once cooked, cool the eggplants to room temperature. Tear or cut the slices into 1-inch strips. Set aside while you prepare the couscous.</p><p>Bring the water to a boil in a medium saucepan. Turn off the heat and stir in the couscous, 2 tablespoons olive oil, and 1 teaspoon salt. Cover the saucepan and let stand until the liquid is absorbed, about 10 minutes. Fluff with a fork.</p><p>Add the garlic, lemon juice and zest, the cumin, coriander, paprika and cayenne to the couscous and stir to combine. Stir in the peppers, parsley, cilantro and mint. If the couscous is too dry, add 1 to 2 tablespoons more olive oil to moisten. Taste for seasoning and add more salt if desired.</p><p>Fold half of the eggplant into the couscous. Spread in a serving bowl or on a platter. Layer the remaining eggplant on top.</p><p>Scatter the feta and mint over the couscous. Garnish with additional lemon zest. Serve at room temperature.</p><p><i>Lynda Balslev is an award-winning writer, cookbook author and recipe developer, and authors the blog TasteFood.</i></p>

entries.title: Shake up your routine with this broccoli salad
entries.summary: <p>Feeling a little broccoli fatigue? This roasted broccoli salad is a delicious way to shake things up. Roasting brings out the broccoli's natural sweetness, toasted almonds add satisfying crunch and sweet raisins provide little bursts of flavor in every bite. A tangy balsamic dressing ties it all together, adding richness with just the right amount of zing.</p><p>This salad keeps well, making it perfect for preparing ahead or packing for a picnic. Whether you're serving it as an easy weeknight side, meal-prepping lunches or adding it to a party spread, this hearty salad is simple to make, satisfying and full of wholesome flavor.</p><h3>Roasted Broccoli Salad With Almonds and Raisins</h3><p><b>Active time:</b> 30 minutes<br><b>Total time:</b> 30 minutes, plus chilling time<br><b>Yield:</b> Serves 4</p><p><b>Ingredients</b></p><p><b>Dressing</b></p><p>2 tablespoons balsamic vinegar<br>2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil<br>1 tablespoon fresh lemon juice<br>1 small garlic clove, grated<br>1 teaspoon runny honey<br>1 teaspoon Dijon mustard<br>1/2 teaspoon kosher salt<br>1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper</p><p>2 medium broccoli heads, about 2 pounds<br>2 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil<br>1/2 teaspoon kosher salt<br>1/4 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper<br>1/4 cup almonds, toasted, coarsely chopped<br>1/4 cup dark or golden raisins<br>1/2 teaspoon finely grated lemon zest</p><p><b>Directions</b></p><p>Whisk the dressing ingredients in a small bowl.</p><p>Trim the broccoli stalks, leaving about 1 inch of the stalk intact. Save the cut stalks for another use.</p><p>Cut the florets into bite-size pieces. Place in a large bowl. Add the oil, salt and black pepper and toss to coat.</p><p>Heat the oven to 425 degrees. Line a rimmed baking sheet with parchment.</p><p>Spread the broccoli on the baking sheet. Transfer to the oven and roast until crisp-tender and charred in spots, about 8 minutes, shaking the pan once or twice. Remove and cool slightly, about 10 minutes.</p><p>Transfer the broccoli to a bowl. Add the almonds, raisins and lemon zest. Drizzle the dressing over the salad and toss to coat. Taste for seasoning.</p><p>Refrigerate the salad for at least 1 hour or up to 4 hours to allow the flavors to develop. Serve chilled or at room temperature.</p><p><i>Lynda Balslev is an award-winning writer, cookbook author and recipe developer, and authors the blog TasteFood.</i></p>

entries.title: Johnson turns up the heat on Springfield to deliver $150M in funding built into Chicago Public School budget
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson vowed Tuesday to do “anything and everything necessary” to keep the Chicago Public Schools afloat, but claimed it’s past time for the Illinois General Assembly to deliver on its commitment to fully fund public schools.</p><p>By declaring a record $1 billion tax-increment-financing surplus to bail out CPS and bankroll a new teachers contract, Johnson said he already has demonstrated his willingness to do what’s necessary to stave off devastating classroom cuts.</p><p>If the General Assembly fails to approve the $150 million increase in education funding built into the nearly $10 billion CPS budget, the mayor made it clear he is prepared to do more of the same.</p><p>But Johnson said his own willingness to put city money where his mouth is should not let Gov. JB Pritzker and state lawmakers off the hook.</p><p>“I’m gonna do anything and everything that’s necessary. But, at some point ... you cannot expect me to solve everybody’s problems and the fact of the matter is I can’t. It’s gonna take partnership,” the mayor said at a City Hall news conference Tuesday.</p><p>“The state of Illinois cannot be okay with the bare minimum when people are starving across this city," he added. "We need our state partners to continue to rise to the occasion. That’s what working people demand. ... They made a commitment to fully fund our schools. That just has to happen.”</p><p>Johnson was asked whether he believes it was legal for the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-school-board/2026/07/30/chicago-school-board-approves-budget-that-reverses-layoffs-but-counts-on-shaky-state-funds" >Chicago Board of Education to approve a budget</a> based on $435 million in “uncommitted funds.”</p><p>He conspicuously avoided answering the question, saying only that the part-elected, part-appointed Board of Education has “gone through their full process to ensure that we’re protecting the classroom.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a entries.title: Chicago high school students can learn about AI at free, 3-day bootcamp this fall
entries.summary: <p>A free three-day AI bootcamp for high school students held in cities around the country since 2019 is expanding to Chicago this fall.</p><p>The Mark Cuban Foundation and the nonprofit group Youth Advocate Programs, Inc. announced Tuesday that <a class="Link" href="https://portal.markcubanai.org/apply" target="_blank" >online registration for the Chicago bootcamp is now open</a>.</p><p></p><p>The camps provide students with an intensive, hands-on introduction to artificial intelligence, one of the fastest-growing technology advancements of the modern era. </p><p>The camps are being held in 31 locations in 19 states and the District of Columbia. Chicago is the only location in Illinois. All locations will be hold their camps on the same consecutive Saturdays — Oct. 31, Nov. 7 and Nov. 14. The program is for high school students of all ages, and is designed to be fully accessible.</p><p>The foundation and the youth nonprofit will provide meals, transportation assistance, and all necessary technology at no cost to participants. Funding comes from the nonprofit, the foundation and other organizations partnering to put on the camps.</p><p>Participants will learn how to use generative AI and machine learning. They also will look at the real-world use of AI in fields such as health care, business, sports, science, and the arts. The curriculum will also tackle the ethical implications of AI, teaching students to navigate issues of bias, transparency, and privacy.</p><p>By the end, students will complete a capstone project that demonstrates their ability to use AI to solve real-world problems.</p><p>“As AI continues to become an undeniable force in all of our lives, it’s crucial that we open the door to this knowledge, especially to young people who want to explore it,” said Mark Cuban, founder of the Mark Cuban Foundation, in a statement. “While technology expands and becomes more advanced, it becomes more critical that we ensure our students are prepared when they apply for schools or jobs in the future.”</p><p>Gary Ivory, president and CEO of Youth Advocate Programs, said the bootcamp helps empower the youth his organization serves.</p><p>“Youth-justice-involved young people and those facing other complex challenges thrive when given opportunities to see and nurture their strengths,” Ivory said in a statement, adding that the camps "will open life-changing educational and economic doors.”</p><p>Applications are accepted only online — at markcubanai.org/students — and must be filled out by the student. More information <a class="Link" href="https://markcubanai.org/students/" target="_blank" >is available here</a>.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://markcubanai.org/students/" target="_blank" ></a></p>

entries.title: Chicago foundation doubles down on Black-led organizations amid DEI rollbacks
entries.summary: <p>While the Trump administration has ignited diversity, equity and inclusion policy rollbacks across corporations, philanthropic foundations and higher education institutions, one Chicago-based foundation has strengthened its commitment to racial justice.</p><p>Grand Victoria Foundation launched a rebrand Tuesday — changing its name to A Movement Advancing Repair and Abundance, or AMARA — that centers investment in Black-led organizations and those with missions that promote racial justice. Despite the new name, AMARA President Sharon Bush said the work is the same.</p><p>“We've been funding this work probably since 2021,” she said.</p><p>One year after the racial reckoning catalyzed by George Floyd’s murder, AMARA commenced a study to identify 81 municipalities across Illinois that had a population of at least 30% Black residents. Bush said the 2021 study allowed the foundation to “learn where people are, so we can figure out how to best focus our efforts.”</p><p>“The board provided us the opening when it said to us in 2020, ‘We want to really be in this for the long-term. We don't want to do temporary measures,’” she said.</p><p>In those early years, when philanthropic institutions and corporations committed to racial justice, AMARA’s board, too, leaned in.</p><p>The board learned about what equity and justice work meant and looked like, and how long would it take.</p><p>“We've had conversations that have been about, what does it mean to focus on Black communities? What does it mean to focus on building the power and agency within those communities, to focus on the things that they think are good and right for their communities?” Bush said.</p><p>The foundation listened to what organizations said they needed and how they could support them. Two key values — abundance and repair — were common themes AMARA heard during their listening sessions. Both values seek to address narratives that Bush said shapes how the Black community is supported and viewed.</p><p>“Repair begins with recognizing that current inequities were shaped by long-standing systems, policies and institutional decisions, not by individual failure,” Bush said. “We think about Black abundance as a way of moving beyond narratives of scarcity and crisis to center more opportunity, wealth, safety, creativity, political power and self-determination in this age.”</p><p>AMARA has a $200 million endowment, with an annual payout rate of 6%-7%, roughly $10 million a year. Some of its funding partners include Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, a national funder, that helped AMARA establish a lot of its work, particularly the 2021 study. It has also partnered with the MacArthur Foundation to build out its narrative change work that will change the stories being told about Black communities. This priority is still being researched.</p><p>Bush said “both funders have been really critical to what our transition has been over the past several years.”</p><p>Thirty-five percent of AMARA’s 2025 grant awards were made to organizations in the Chicago area, according to a foundation spokesperson, Landon Williams. KOCO Chicago, Southside Together, Black Roots Alliance, and Organized Communities Against Deportation are among its Chicago-area grantees. Bush said investing in immigration may “seem to be a non-Black issue, [but] underneath, it is,” pointing out that there are Black immigrants. She said, “These other organizations … might have different kind of leadership, but they hold centering Black power within the ways in which they work.”</p><p>AMARA’s rebrand will be celebratedThursday at the Obama Presidential Center, when Chicago African Americans in Philanthropy celebrates Black Philanthropy Month.</p>
